title: Food Chains & Energy Flow
hook: Energy enters most ecosystems as sunlight, gets captured by plants, and flows up the menu — but it leaks away at every bite, so the chain stays short.
key_points: Producers (plants, algae) capture energy; consumers eat to get it secondhand.
A food web is the tangle of interconnected food chains in an ecosystem.
Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level — the rest is lost mostly as heat.
That energy loss is why top predators are few and chains rarely run more than 4-5 links.
content_html: Energy is the real currency of an ecosystem, and a food chain traces its path. It almost always starts with producers — plants, algae, and some bacteria — that capture sunlight through photosynthesis and lock it into sugar. Animals can't do this, so they eat to get their energy secondhand: herbivores eat producers, and carnivores eat the herbivores. In reality these chains crisscross into a food web, since most creatures eat, and are eaten by, several others.
extra_html: The catch is that energy doesn't transfer cleanly. At each step, an organism spends most of the energy it takes in on simply living — moving, growing, staying warm — and much is lost as heat. As a rough rule, only about 10% of the energy at one level makes it into the next. That leak has a big consequence: the higher you go, the less energy is left to go around, which is why ecosystems support vast numbers of plants but only a handful of top predators, and why food chains rarely stretch beyond four or five links. Khan Academy illustrates the pyramid of energy and where it all goes.

related.title: Photosynthesis
related.hook: Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil, and using only sunlight, build sugar — releasing the oxygen you're breathing right now.

related.title: Ecosystems & Interdependence
related.hook: An ecosystem is a community of living things plus their environment, all so tangled together that pulling one thread can shake the whole web.

flashcards.prompt: What is a producer in a food chain?
flashcards.back_html: An organism that makes its own food and captures energy — like a plant or alga doing photosynthesis. Producers are the base every food chain rests on.

flashcards.prompt: Roughly how much energy passes from one feeding level to the next?

choices.text: About 10% — most is lost, largely as heat
All of it — energy transfers perfectly

flashcards.explanation_html: Only around a tenth of the energy at one level is captured by the next; the rest is used up or lost as heat, which is why food chains stay short.

flashcards.prompt: Why are there usually far fewer top predators than plants in an ecosystem?

choices.text: So much energy is lost at each step that little remains to support high levels
Predators choose to keep their numbers low
Plants are simply easier to count

flashcards.explanation_html: Each transfer wastes most of the available energy, so the amount left shrinks sharply up the chain — supporting only a few top predators.
